# Preface {.unnumbered}

*A Python Companion to Intermediate Macroeconomics* is a set of computational notebooks. Each notebook takes one chapter of an
intermediate macroeconomics course and rebuilds its figures in Python, so that you can
**see the data** and **play with the models**.

## How to use this book

- **On this website** you can read every chapter, see all the figures, hover over the data
  points, and move the precomputed sliders under each model figure.
- **In Google Colab** you can run the code yourself. Click the *Open in Colab* badge at the
  top of a chapter, then choose *Runtime → Run all*. In Colab every model figure gets live
  sliders and buttons that recompute the model as you move them, and every "Your turn"
  exercise can be tried in an empty code cell.
- No installation is needed: Colab already has `numpy`, `pandas`, `plotly` and `ipywidgets`.
  The data are read directly from this book's GitHub repository.
- **New to Python or Colab?** Start with
  [Appendix A](notebooks/appA-google-colab-python-and-data-science-libraries.ipynb). It is a guided tour of
  Colab, with screenshots, a short introduction to Python, and the data science libraries used in the book.
- **Want the data yourself?**
  [Appendix B](notebooks/appB-accessing-macroeconomic-data-with-python.ipynb) shows how to download
  macroeconomic data straight from FRED, the World Bank, the IMF, the ECB, Eurostat, the OECD, the Penn World
  Table, the Maddison Project and Our World in Data.

## About the figures

The notebooks follow the chapters of Charles I. Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th edition, W. W. Norton](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612). They are an independent
teaching companion, not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or the publisher, and they are not a substitute
for the textbook.

Every figure is **our own adaptation**, drawn with our own code: data figures are **inspired by** the
textbook's figures and rebuilt from public data, usually updated to the latest year and extended to other
countries; model figures are **adapted from** the textbook's diagrams, with our own parameter values, layout and
interactive controls. None is a copy of an original figure. A **Sources** note directly below every figure names
the textbook figure that inspired it and links to the data sources, so you can open them and explore the data
yourself. A crosswalk table at the top of every chapter lists the textbook figure behind each notebook figure.
